title: Instant-payment fraud controls work differently when fees change who can use the system
summary: A central payments operator can coordinate fraud prevention across sending and receiving institutions, but that alone need not produce the socially preferred outcome. In this Bank of Canada staff working paper, Yuteng Cheng, Charles Kahn and Francisco Rivadeneyra show that the comparison also turns on which payment sizes can use the instant system and how its costs are recovered. A uniform fee can make a small, socially worthwhile transfer unattractive to the payer. In some circumstances, easier access under decentralized pricing can outweigh the disadvantages of splitting prevention incentives between banks. These are results from a theoretical model, not estimated loss rates or a recommendation for a particular payment system.

Immediate settlement creates convenience and compresses the interval in which a suspected scam can be interrupted. The sending institution can screen a payment while the receiving institution can monitor its destination. Both controls affect the probability that a fraudulent payment succeeds. Prevention uses resources, and the expected monetary loss increases with transaction size. The model assumes diminishing additional convenience from sending a larger transfer instantly and sufficient value for small transfers. Its social planner admits transfers from zero up to an efficient upper limit and chooses preventive effort on both sides. That upper limit for using the payment rail is distinct from a cap on compensating a victim after fraud (sections 2–3).

A centralized operator may seek adoption, payer surplus subject to breaking even, or profit. With a flat fee, recovering prevention costs and expected losses across all users can price out the smallest payments. Removing that lower cutoff and requiring the efficient maximum payment size lets a coordinated operator deliver efficient prevention under the conditions derived in the paper. More flexible, size-dependent fees can also remove the small-payment barrier, but an operator maximizing usage can still cross-subsidize transactions whose social cost exceeds their benefit if it is required only to break even in aggregate (section 4 and appendix A).

In the decentralized model, competitive sending banks set the customer fee while the costs incurred by receiving banks do not enter it directly. If each bank pays a fraction of fraud losses, each captures only a fraction of the benefit from better controls. Holding eligible payment sizes fixed, the preferred split depends on how much each side can improve prevention at the margin and how its costs change as controls tighten. An equal split is optimal only when the adjusted cost curvatures match. A relatively inflexible receiving-side prevention technology favours placing more liability on senders if they can respond more cheaply. Minimizing fraud dollars is a different objective from maximizing welfare once the resources devoted to prevention are counted (section 5, proposition 7).

The numerical example isolates pricing by making both sides’ prevention responses relatively inflexible and fixing a common upper cap. Figure 1 shows decentralized provision can deliver greater welfare where receiver monitoring is costly and the sender bears a low liability share. Small payments continue to use the system because the sender’s price excludes much of the cost that a centralized flat fee must recover. The figure is an illustration of how the ranking can reverse, not a calibration to Canada or an estimated optimal loss split.

The extensions change the interpretation of reimbursement. More generous reimbursement can improve participation while reducing the incentive for payers to take care above the reimbursement cap. If uncompensated victims experience additional harm, such as loss of trust or time, reimbursement has a direct social benefit too. Allowing potential fraudsters to choose whether to participate makes effective controls more valuable because fewer attacks may be attempted. These extensions reinforce the need to evaluate access, bank effort and consumer protection together (section 6).

questions.question: Which institution can reduce expected losses most efficiently at the margin?
questions.detail: The paper’s liability rule depends on relative prevention costs and their responsiveness, quantities it does not estimate. Examine payment providers’ operating records and carefully evaluated changes in screening or monitoring intensity, alongside attempted and realized losses. Compare like payment sizes and allow for changes in attack volume. These inputs would help assess how a different loss split affects bank costs and whether it buys meaningful protection.

questions.question: How many worthwhile small payments would a cost-recovering fee displace?
questions.detail: The governance ranking changes when a flat charge excludes small transfers. Obtain scheme-level transaction distributions, provider fee schedules and payer switching evidence where prices or transfer limits changed. Compare comparable transactions across the instant rail and its alternatives. Measuring the take-up response and the value users place on speed is necessary before treating lower adoption or a lower fraud total as evidence of better design.

questions.question: How does reimbursement change behaviour and the harm borne by users?
questions.detail: The extensions allow both weaker payer precaution and a direct benefit from avoiding uncompensated harm. Compare contemporaneous claims, recovery outcomes, user surveys and transfer activity around reimbursement thresholds under existing scheme rules. Separate variation in transaction size from differences in prior customer behaviour. The evidence would inform loss provisions and consumer access while distinguishing genuine protection from a change in which party records the loss.
